html:
"Hindu kingdoms" is the map's broad label, used in fourteen snapshots from 500 BCE to 1715, for parts of South Asia held by many small Hindu states that the source data does not name one by one. Where it sits changes with the period.

  • 500 to 300 BCE, it covers much of the north: the kingdoms and republics of the Mahajanapadas before and around the rise of Magadha.
  • About 300 BCE to 400 CE, it covers the far south, the Tamil lands of the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas, known from Sangam poetry and from Roman trade at ports such as Muziris. Around 100 CE it also covers the Ganges plain, held by local kings in the centuries between the Mauryas and the rise of the Guptas.
  • 600 to 700, it covers northern and north-western India after the Guptas: states such as Harsha's kingdom at Kannauj and smaller Rajput and other dynasties.
  • 1100, it marks Rajasthan, the Punjab hills and Kashmir, held by Rajput and other dynasties after the Hindu Shahis fell to Ghazni.
  • 1700 and 1715, it is the far south again: the Nayaks of Madurai and other successors of Vijayanagara, and Malabar kingdoms such as Travancore, outside the reach of the Mughal Empire.

What these states had in common was not one religion but a shared order: kings who claimed a Kshatriya role, gave land to Brahmins, built temples to Shiva and Vishnu, and used Sanskrit or regional languages at court. Buddhists and Jains often lived in the same kingdoms. The map's label is a placeholder for a crowded political world of shifting borders, tribute and alliances.
sum: "Hindu kingdoms" is the map's broad label, used in fourteen snapshots from 500 BCE to 1715, for parts of South Asia held by many small Hindu states that the source data does not name one by one. Where it sits changes with the period.
